title: Homogeneous Systems Ax = 0
quickIdea: Ax = 0 always has the trivial solution, so it is never inconsistent. The only question is whether a non-zero solution exists, and that happens exactly when the rank is below the number of unknowns.
remember: Ax = 0 is always consistent: x = 0 satisfies it for every A. It therefore has either one solution (only x = 0) or infinitely many, never none and never a finite number above one.
A non-trivial solution exists if and only if rank(A) < n, that is if and only if nullity is positive.
For a square n x n A this reads: a non-trivial solution exists if and only if |A| = 0.
If m < n, a homogeneous system always has a non-trivial solution, because rank(A) is at most m < n.
The solution set of Ax = 0 is a subspace, so sums and scalar multiples of solutions are solutions. If b is non-zero and Ax = b has at least one solution, then it has infinitely many.

example.prompt: For which p, q, r has px + qy + rz = 0, qx + ry + pz = 0, rx + py + qz = 0 a non-trivial solution?
example.work: The coefficient matrix has determinant 3pqr - p^3 - q^3 - r^3, which factors as -(p + q + r)(p^2 + q^2 + r^2 - pq - qr - rp), and the second factor equals half of ((p-q)^2 + (q-r)^2 + (r-p)^2), which is zero only when p = q = r.
example.answer: A non-trivial solution exists exactly when p + q + r = 0 or p = q = r. This is GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.33, whose correct option is 'p + q + r = 0 or p = q = r'.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.33 is the determinant form of the test; GATE CSE 1996 Q.1.7 checks that you know a homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations always has infinitely many solutions; GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.39 asks how many independent non-trivial solutions are guaranteed.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can a homogeneous system be inconsistent?
variations.why: The right-hand side is the zero vector, which is in the column space of every matrix, so the two ranks can never differ.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 3 x 3 with |A| = 0. Does Ax = b have a solution for a given non-zero b?
variations.answer: It depends on b, and the answer is not settled by the determinant.
variations.why: The determinant says only that the homogeneous system has a non-zero solution. Consistency of the non-homogeneous system is a statement about b, checked by comparing ranks.

trap.what: Transferring the singular-matrix conclusion from Ax = 0 to Ax = b.
trap.why: The free-solution guarantee belongs to the homogeneous system, whose right-hand side is already in the column space. A non-zero b may sit outside it.
trap.counterexample: A = [[1,1],[1,1]] has |A| = 0, so x + y = 0, x + y = 0 has the non-trivial solution (1,-1); the same A with b = (1,2) gives x + y = 1 and x + y = 2, which has no solution.

check.question: A is 4 x 3. Can Ax = 0 have only the trivial solution?
check.explanation: The test is rank against the number of unknowns, not the number of equations. Four equations in three unknowns with full column rank force every unknown to zero.
